analysis.one_liner: Requires big social media and gaming platforms to protect kids online and lets users turn off manipulative feeds.
analysis.headline: A kids' online safety bill with 64 bipartisan cosponsors cleared a House committee by voice vote in September 2024 but never got a House floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make the largest online platforms and games legally responsible for preventing harms to kids, such as anxiety, depression, compulsive use, cyberbullying, sexual exploitation, and ads for drugs, tobacco, alcohol, and gambling. It would require platforms to give minors and parents simple settings to turn off addictive features like infinite scrolling and autoplay, and to opt out of personalized recommendation algorithms. It would also let any user switch to a plain, chronological feed instead of an algorithmically ranked one, require yearly independent audits of how platforms affect kids, and let the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers using social media, games, and streaming apps, plus their parents, who get easy-to-use controls over what their kids see and buy. All users gain from the right to turn off algorithmically manipulated feeds.

how_it_helps.text: The largest online companies (those with $2.5 billion or more in revenue, or 150 million or more users) would have a legal duty to use reasonable care to prevent harms to minors, including anxiety, depression, eating disorders, substance use, suicidal behavior, compulsive usage, cyberbullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol.

Platforms would have to give known minors accessible safeguards by default: the most protective safety settings unless a parent changes them, the ability to turn off infinite scrolling, autoplay, notifications, and other engagement-driving features, and the option to opt out of personalized recommendation systems and see content chronologically.
Parents would get tools to manage a child's account, restrict purchases and in-game microtransactions, and view and limit time spent, with these tools enabled by default for children under 13.

Any user of a covered platform could switch between an algorithmic feed and an 'input-transparent' (non-manipulated) feed, and platforms could not charge users different prices for choosing the unmanipulated feed.

Platforms with more than 10 million U.S. users would have to publish annual public reports on risks of harm to minors, based on an independent third-party audit with full access to the platform's systems.
The FTC could enforce the law as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general could sue platforms over the safeguards, disclosure, and transparency requirements.

analysis.who_pays: The largest social media, gaming, and streaming companies, which would bear compliance costs, independent audits, new liability, and some loss of engagement-driven ad revenue from minors. Smaller covered platforms would face lighter but real obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large online platforms and game makers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require age verification, but it grades platforms' legal knowledge of a user's age, with large companies liable if they 'should have known' a user was a minor. To avoid liability, platforms would likely infer ages, meaning more data collection about all users.

The duty of care covers broad mental-health harms, which could push platforms to restrict or remove lawful content and features for minors to avoid liability, limiting what young people can access online.

State attorneys general would gain new power to sue platforms over safeguards and disclosures; the bill bars them from using the mental-health duty of care as the basis of a state-law claim, but their enforcement of other sections raises the stakes of compliance choices.

Obligations fall on any platform 'reasonably likely to be used by a minor,' and on mid-sized companies (about $200 million in revenue or more with 200,000 or more users) under a willful-disregard standard, so smaller companies face compliance costs, though the heaviest duty of care applies only to the giants.
Parental monitoring tools could be used to surveil teenagers; the bill softens this by requiring clear notice to the minor when parental tools are in effect and what settings were applied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to children's safety and to any user tired of engagement-optimized feeds are substantial and concrete, and the heaviest obligations are aimed at companies that can afford them. The main costs are compliance burdens and the risk that platforms over-restrict minors' access to content or collect more data to guess ages; on balance the protections for kids and all users outweigh these costs, though the age-inference problem is a real design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved the bill by voice vote in September 2024, but the House never brought it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Gus Bilirakis (R-FL) introduced the bill on April 9, 2024 with bipartisan original cosponsors including Reps. Castor (D-FL), Houchin (R-IN), Schrier (D-WA), and Bucshon (R-IN).
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee on the day of introduction.
It went to the Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee on May 20, 2024 and was forwarded to the full committee by voice vote on May 23.
The full Energy and Commerce Committee held a markup on September 18, 2024 and ordered the bill to be reported, as amended, by voice vote.
No further action followed: the bill was never reported to the House floor and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media and gaming companies, which avoided a legal duty of care toward minors, mandatory safety defaults, annual independent audits, state attorneys general enforcement, and a user right to switch off engagement-optimizing algorithms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and gaming companies

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split exactly evenly, 32 House Democrats and 32 House Republicans, both subcommittee and full committee advanced it by voice vote, and the only visible opposition came from the House's failure to schedule a vote rather than a recorded party split.

industries.industry: Large social media platforms (companies with $2.5B+ revenue or 150M+ users)
industries.note: They would face a legal duty of care to prevent harms to minors, the most protective safety settings on by default, annual independent audits, and lawsuits from the FTC and state attorneys general. Their ad revenue depends on maximizing time spent, including by minors, so the bill directly curbs their core growth mechanics.

industries.industry: Online video game companies with in-game purchases and player communication
industries.note: Online games are covered platforms, and the bill defines microtransactions, including 'surprise mechanics' and in-game items, as targets for parental purchase restrictions. It also bans interfaces designed to manipulate users' choices, which reaches loot-box-style monetization aimed at young players.

Services whose content is preselected rather than user-generated are deemed compliant if they meet lighter requirements, such as kid profiles, purchase restrictions, and not serving alcohol, tobacco, or gambling ads to known minors. User-generated platforms like TikTok or YouTube face the full weight of the law; traditional streamers largely do not.

industries.industry: Mid-sized online platforms (roughly $200M revenue and 200,000+ users)
industries.note: They escape the giant companies' duty of care but are still covered platforms for safeguards and parental tools, and they are liable for a minor's harm if they acted in willful disregard of a user's age. Compliance costs are real but the heaviest obligations apply only to the giants.
